summary: Teach the bar model (tape diagram) as the workhorse for ratio and proportion. A ratio like 3:2 becomes 3 equal blocks beside 2 equal blocks; once the value of ONE block is known, every share, scaling and percentage answer is read off the picture. Build three habits: (1) draw bars matching the relationship, (2) find the value of one block (known amount ÷ number of blocks it covers — e.g. total ÷ all blocks when the total is given, or one share ÷ that share's blocks when a part is given), (3) read off what is asked — with the equal-unit convention (every block the same size) made firm first. Progress from concrete cubes/counters to a drawn, labelled bar to the numeric calculation, and always draw before calculating so problem structure is visible rather than guessed from key words. Constructing a model is the core objective; reading a prepared model is a valuable scaffold toward it.
misconceptions: Draws blocks of unequal size, so the model no longer represents equal units
Sets up part-to-whole when the problem is part-to-part (draws a bar of 3 for a 3:2 ratio and treats the 2 as part of it), or vice versa
Jumps to arithmetic without finding the value of one block, so the diagram is decorative rather than a solving tool
Maps the wrong quantity to the wrong bar, or forgets which bar is which after drawing

activities.title: Build the tape diagram: draw, find one block, read off
steps: Given '£20 shared in the ratio 3:2', build two bars — 3 equal blocks beside 2 equal blocks — keeping every block the same width.
Place a brace spanning all 5 blocks and label it with the total, £20.
Find the value of one block by dividing the total by the number of blocks: £20 ÷ 5 = £4.
Fill every block with £4, then read off the two shares: 3 × £4 = £12 and 2 × £4 = £8; check they add back to £20.
Toggle the same ratio between part-to-part twin bars (3 and 2) and a part-to-whole single bar of 5, and say which layout the question needs.
Repeat independently for a new problem: share £18 in the ratio 5:1 — six equal blocks in two bars (5 and 1), brace £18, one block = £3, shares £15 and £3.
Re-read one of your diagrams as a proportion: 'what fraction of the money is the shaded bar?' (e.g. 3 out of 5).
activities.insight: Each block is an equal unit standing for the same amount; dividing the whole by the number of blocks gives one block's value, and from that single fact every share and proportion can be read straight off the picture without a memorised rule.

activities.title: Concrete first: build the ratio with cubes, then draw it
steps: Lay out coloured cubes or counters for a part-to-part ratio — e.g. 1 cube of concentrate for every 4 cubes of water.
Count the total cubes and share a given total across them so each cube (block) gets an equal value.
Redraw the same arrangement as a labelled bar diagram, matching one block to one cube.
State in words what each block stands for before doing any arithmetic.
activities.insight: The drawn block is a shorthand for an equal physical unit; moving from cubes to the drawn bar preserves the equal-unit meaning rather than inventing a new rule.

activities.title: Read a worked bar model (scaffold)
steps: Study a labelled '£20 shared 3:2' diagram and, part by part, state what each feature means: a single block, the 3-section, the 2-section, the brace, any shading.
Reveal and confirm: one block = £20 ÷ 5 = £4; the 3-section = £12; the brace shows the whole = £20.
Explain back, in your own words, how the one-block value was found and how each share follows from it.
activities.insight: Fluent reading of a prepared diagram — knowing what every block, brace and shaded section stands for — supports constructing your own model, which this scaffold then leads into.

activities.title: Match, read and sketch (assessment-style practice)
steps: Match bar diagrams to the worded problems they represent.
Read a quantity off a labelled bar, watching for traps: a distractor assuming unequal blocks, and a distractor confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole.
Sketch the blocks for a given ratio (e.g. draw the layout for sharing a stated total in a stated ratio).
activities.insight: Interpreting and translating between words and bar models — and noticing where equal-unit or part/whole choices go wrong — shows command of the representation beyond surface recognition.

activities.title: Compare the bar model with tables and double number lines
steps: Solve the same problem with a bar model and then with a ratio table or double number line.
For a fixed-total sharing problem and for a scaling-up-a-rate problem, decide which representation is most useful and say why.
Discuss with a mentor or partner: 'What does each block stand for? What is the total? Which tool fits this question best?'
activities.insight: Different representations often suit different questions — bar models are especially clear for sharing a fixed total, while tables and double number lines are often convenient for scaling a rate (though each can solve both) — and being able to choose and justify a representation shows flexible understanding.

checkQuestion: Here is a bar model: two bars, one made of 3 equal blocks and one made of 2 equal blocks, with a brace over all of them labelled '£20'. First, tell me what this diagram is showing. Then draw me a new bar model for sharing £18 in the ratio 5:1.
checkAnswer: The diagram shows a quantity of £20 shared in the ratio 3:2 — 5 equal blocks in total, each worth £20÷5 = £4, so the shares are £12 and £8. For the new one: six equal blocks in two bars (5 and 1), brace £18, one block = £3, shares £15 and £3.
